one_line_definition: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) lets an AI chatbot look up relevant information from a trusted source first, then use it to write its answer.
why_it_matters: It makes AI answers more accurate, current and checkable without the cost of retraining the model, and lets companies point AI at their own documents.
pain_point: You ask a chatbot about something recent or about your own company's documents, and it confidently gives an out-of-date or made-up answer, because its knowledge froze when training ended.
how_it_works: Your documents are turned into numbers (embeddings) and stored in a vector database, like a searchable library.
Your question is also turned into numbers and matched against that library.
The most relevant passages are pulled out (retrieved).
Those passages are added to your question (the prompt is augmented).
The AI writes its answer from them (generation) and can cite the sources.

key_facts.fact: The term RAG was coined in a 2020 paper led by Patrick Lewis, with coauthors from Facebook AI Research, University College London and New York University.
The paper 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks' was first submitted to arXiv on 22 May 2020.
The original RAG models used a dense vector index of Wikipedia as their non-parametric memory, accessed with a neural retriever.
RAG models generated more specific, diverse and factual language than a parametric-only baseline.
LLM training data is static, which gives the model a knowledge cut-off date; LLMs can present false or out-of-date information.
RAG improves LLM output without retraining the model, making it a cost-effective way to add new data.
The user query is converted to a vector, matched against a vector database, and the retrieved data is added to the prompt before the LLM answers.
RAG gives models sources they can cite, like footnotes, so users can check claims; it reduces (does not eliminate) the chance of hallucination.
Lewis apologized for the unflattering acronym, saying no one had a better name when the paper was written.

analogies: A judge who sends a court clerk to the law library for the exact precedent before ruling (NVIDIA's analogy).
An open-book exam instead of answering from memory.
Footnotes in a research paper that let you check the claim.
misconceptions: RAG does not retrain or change the model; it only adds retrieved text to the prompt.
RAG reduces hallucinations but does not eliminate them; answers are only as good as the retrieved sources.
RAG is not one product; it is a general technique that works with nearly any LLM and data source.
